title: Tax Laws Amendment (Temporary Flood and Cyclone Reconstruction Levy) Bill 2011

divisions.question: That these bills be now read a second time. That these bills be now read a second time.
That these bills be now read a third time.

speeches.speaker: Don Farrell
speeches.brief: The speaker moved to expedite consideration of the Tax Laws Amendment (Temporary Flood and Cyclone Reconstruction Levy) Bill 2011 and the Income Tax Rates Amendment (Temporary Flood and Cyclone Reconstruction Levy) Bill 2011, which introduce a temporary levy for the 2011-12 income year, citing urgency to finalise administrative arrangements before 30 June 2011.

speeches.speaker: Don Farrell
speeches.brief: The government introduced a temporary flood reconstruction levy for the 2011-12 financial year, applying 0.5% to taxable income between $50,001 and $100,000 and 1% above $100,000, to raise $1.8 billion toward an estimated $5.6 billion in flood and cyclone recovery costs, with exemptions for disaster-affected individuals and half of all taxpayers paying nothing. The opposition argued the levy was unnecessary due to government waste and proposed alternative budget cuts, while the Greens supported the levy as a progressive measure but called for long-term disaster planning and climate change action.

speeches.speaker: Dana Wortley
speeches.brief: The government argued for a temporary flood reconstruction levy of $1.8 billion, applying a 0.5% rate on incomes $50,000–$100,000 and 1% above that, with exemptions for disaster-affected individuals. Opposition speakers opposed the levy, claiming the government could have funded rebuilding through budget cuts instead and citing past waste in programs such as pink batts and Building the Education Revolution.

speeches.speaker: Joe Ludwig
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the Temporary Flood and Cyclone Reconstruction Levy bills, arguing they are necessary for rebuilding Queensland and other disaster-affected regions after floods and Cyclone Yasi. The levy applies only to incomes over $50,000, is temporary and modest, and will raise $1.8 billion, with $3.8 billion from spending cuts.

speeches.speaker: Catryna Bilyk
speeches.brief: The speaker argued the temporary flood and cyclone reconstruction levy is a fair, one-off measure for the 2011–12 financial year, exempting those earning under $50,000 and disaster-affected individuals, with rates of 0.5% for incomes $50,001–$100,000 and 1% above $100,000; the government also announced $2 billion in advance payments to Queensland, deferrals of infrastructure projects, and appointments including Major General Michael Slater to lead the Queensland Reconstruction Authority and John Fahey to head a reconstruction inspectorate.

speeches.speaker: Fiona Nash
speeches.brief: The coalition opposed the temporary flood and cyclone reconstruction levy, arguing it was unnecessary due to government waste and mismanagement, citing $1.7 billion in BER blow-outs, $2.4 billion in pink batts costs, and other examples; the government and supporting crossbenchers defended the levy as a temporary, progressive measure raising $1.8 billion to fund $5.6 billion in rebuilding, applying only to incomes over $50,000 for one year.

speeches.speaker: Carol Brown
speeches.brief: The speaker presented the Standing Committee on Economics Legislation Committee's report on the Tax Laws Amendment (Temporary Flood and Cyclone Reconstruction Levy) Bill 2011, along with the Hansard record and related documents.

speeches.speaker: Nick Xenophon
speeches.brief: Senator Xenophon announced new provisions in the Natural Disaster Relief and Recovery Arrangements requiring states to have adequate capital or insurance, with independent assessments and potential funding reductions for non-compliance. The opposition argued the flood levy unfairly targets individuals rather than corporations, while the government defended it as progressive and noted previous coalition levies.

speeches.speaker: Ian Macdonald
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the flood levy unfairly taxes individuals while exempting multinational corporations like BHP, Xstrata and Rio Tinto, and demanded the minister clarify which natural disaster victims are exempt, citing contradictions between the Treasury website and the Prime Minister's office on whether bushfire and other non-flood disaster victims must pay.

speeches.speaker: Mathias Cormann
speeches.brief: The opposition argued the flood levy is an unfair flat tax on individuals earning over $50,000 that exempts corporations, and they will vote against it; the minister eventually confirmed that all Australians receiving natural disaster assistance payments would be exempt from the levy.
